A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICAI research, retaining the problem formulation, core algorithm, and original experiments. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original preference-reconstruction experiments on synthetic, AlpacaEval, and Chatbot Arena data, including cross-model transfer and constitution-length sensitivity results.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds PRISM group experiments, bias analysis, HH-RLHF annotation scaling, component ablations, and additional baseline evaluations.

M1.justification: The five-step ICAI algorithm and original prompts remain substantively unchanged. v2 adds limited application-specific adaptations: manual selection and retesting of candidate bias principles (Section 4.5, Appendix F.2), and generation/voting prompts focused on the final conversation turn for HH-RLHF (Appendix F.3).

E1.justification: Beyond the retained synthetic, AlpacaEval, and individual Chatbot Arena experiments, v2 evaluates demographic-group preferences using PRISM, helpfulness and harmlessness on Anthropic HH-RLHF, and newer Chatbot Arena Kaggle conversations for bias analysis. These substantially broaden the represented populations and preference scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds flipped Default, a PopAlign-based annotator, pretrained PairRM, and fine-tuned PairRM to the synthetic and AlpacaEval comparisons (Tables 4–5). It also adds the Default annotator to the Chatbot Arena cross-user comparison (Figure 6, Table 6), where v1 compared only the two users' constitutions.

E3.justification: v2 retains the original experiments but adds substantial evaluation protocols: 324/324 AlpacaEval training/test samples, 100/1,000 samples per HH-RLHF task, and bias evaluation across 13,253 preferences using relevance and conditional accuracy. New PairRM experiments introduce fine-tuning and validation controls, while PRISM evaluates selected groups without a training/test split.

E4.justification: v1's constitution-length, transfer, and individual-user analyses are retained. v2 adds four component variations covering simplified generation, multi-preference generation, deduplication removal, and testing/filtering removal (Table 3), alongside sample-scale sensitivity and substantive bias-detection and demographic-group case studies.

E5.justification: Retained experiments preserve six-seed mean/standard-deviation reporting and four seeds for model transfer. v2 specifies three complete-pipeline seeds for HH-RLHF and explicitly reports PairRM using one seed without dispersion statistics (Appendices F.3 and F.8). These are limited reporting additions, not evidence of increased runs for existing results.

E6.justification: Original numerical results are retained, but substantial new results appear. Table 7 reports 77.22% agreement for PRISM Group A's constitution versus 58.33% for Default. Table 10 adds the larger AlpacaEval setting, with GPT-4o constitutional agreement of 61.47% versus 33.80% for Default. Added comparisons also expose limitations: flipped Default reaches 72.31% versus ICAI's retained 66.41% on small unaligned AlpacaEval (Table 5).

T1.justification: Equation 1 retains the same agreement-maximization objective and constitution-length constraint. Changing p(c) to p_M(c) merely makes the already stated model dependence explicit. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the claimed contributions to demonstrated real-data bias detection and interpretation of demographic-group preferences. v1 emphasized dataset and individual-user constitutions, with bias detection mainly presented as a prospective application. The compression formulation and initial algorithm remain central, but the claimed application scope broadens substantially.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of group preferences, component ablations, and helpfulness/harmlessness transfer. Beyond v1's existing non-causality and lossy-compression caveats, it explains incomplete bias detection, difficulty identifying subtle social biases, downstream bias amplification, demographic cherry-picking risks, and the interpretability–accuracy tradeoff (Section 6, Ethics Statement, Appendices C and F). Some new ablation interpretations contradict Table 3.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies the clustering embedding model and supplies substantial details for added experiments: GPT-4o-mini's version, HH-RLHF sampling and prompt adaptations, PairRM's checkpoint and fine-tuning settings, and the adapted PopAlign prompt/configuration (Appendices A, D, F, G). Both versions already provide source-code access and the original prompts; those are retained disclosures.

R1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B substantially expand positioning through distribution-description research and detailed comparisons with concurrent ICAI, I3CAI, SPADE, VibeCheck, PopAlign, and rule-based rewards. v2 explicitly acknowledges Kostolansky's concurrent, identically named ICAI formulation and distinguishes its objective and procedure from this work.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, motivation, and experimental narrative, including explicit AlpacaEval research questions. It reorganizes the appendices, moves detailed Chatbot Arena and transfer material out of the main text, redistributes related work, and introduces separate ethics and reproducibility statements. These are substantial structural and explanatory revisions.

P2.justification: v2 adds PRISM, HH-RLHF, and sample-scaling plots, bias and ablation tables, and expanded baseline tables. The Chatbot Arena plot gains Default bars and moves to the appendix; the Claude transfer plot also moves there. Captions, table organization, typography, and the conference page layout are extensively revised, while the central schematics remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited baseline comparisons and absence of component ablations, making ICAI's strengths and weaknesses more assessable. New application studies, implementation details, and explicit applicability limits strengthen the paper beyond merely adding results. The new ablation prose sometimes contradicts Table 3, particularly on deduplication trends, which weakens that discussion. Nevertheless, the broader comparative evidence and clearer limitations provide a substantial net improvement.
